data.title: Mattel's New CEO Wants to Win in Toys, Not Movies — Market Talk
data.description: Roger Lynch's public debut as Mattel's chief executive highlighted what JPMorgan analysts see as his vision for the company's turnaround. "Indeed, his first priority is to 'strengthen the brands and win in toys,' highlighting the long-duration success of Hot Wheels as the guide path for fixing Barbie," the analysts say in a research note. "Drive innovation, his second priority, strongly relates to the first, with capital discipline the final pillar." Noticeably, Lynch's vision for the toy company doesn't seem to include the Disney-eque ambitions of his predecessor, Ynon Kreiz, they add. Under Kreiz's leadership, Mattel spent years trying to transform into a toy and entertainment company, partnering with movie studios to bring its brands to the big screen while also expanding into digital games and live experiences. (connor.hart@wsj.com)

data.title: Creative Planning Snags $2.2 Billion Investment Advisor Firm Serving Central New York — Barrons.com
data.description:
By Kenneth Corbin

Creative Planning has acquired Rockbridge Investment Management, a registered investment advisor firm based in Syracuse, N.Y., that manages $2.2 billion in client assets. The deal, announced Wednesday, closed on Monday.

Rockbridge was founded in 1991 and caters to a variety of retail and institutional clients. On the retail side, the firm offers retirement and estate planning and advises on insurance and tax issues.

"Rockbridge has built its reputation in central New York on in-depth financial planning and a thoughtful client experience, and that commitment mirrors how we approach our work," says Creative Planning CEO Peter Mallouk.

The acquisition brings eight advisors and 15 support staffers to Creative Planning, a prolific acquirer and one of the largest RIAs in the country. Based in Overland Park, Kan., Creative Planning landed at No. 2 on Barron's 2026 list of mega RIAs.

Creative Planning announced 10 acquisitions in 2025, with only four firms tallying more deals, according to DeVoe & Co., a consultancy and investment bank that tracks deal activity in the RIA sector. The firm has closed seven deals so far this year and has two more in the pipeline, according to a spokeswoman.

Rockbridge is a fee-only firm that primarily serves retail clients, saying in a July regulatory filing that it works with just over 1,200 nonhigh-net worth individuals and 316 high-net-worth individuals, who account for the largest share of its assets under management. The firm also works with several dozen institutions, including businesses and charitable organizations.

In a joint statement, Rockbridge CEO Patrick Rohe and Managing Partner David Carroll say that they clicked with Mallouk in their first meeting. They say they "share his vision for where the RIA industry is headed," which includes offering clients more services under one roof.

"For years, clients have asked us for coordinated services like estate planning and tax preparation," they say, and joining Creative Planning will provide their advisors with more resources and a deep bench of experts including accountants and estate-planning professionals.

This content was created by Barron's, which is operated by Dow Jones & Co. Barron's is published independently from Dow Jones Newswires and The Wall Street Journal.

data.title: Airbnb AI Products Gain Traction, Cut Costs — Market Talk
data.description: 13:02 ET--Airbnb's AI products are gaining traction, Raymond James analysts say. The company launched an AI natural-language search across its homes, experiences and services platforms, alongside AI-generated listing summaries and filters. Early adoption is strongest among younger travelers, the analysts say. Airbnb's AI customer services resolved about 40% of all customer support issues without human intervention in the latest quarter, the analysts say. That was up from 33% the quarter before. Meanwhile, the customer support cost per booking declined 17% year-over-year, driven largely by AI, the analysts say. Airbnb is developing a travel agent set to launch in the first half of next year. (katherine.hamilton@wsj.com)

data.title: USDA to launch AI tool to check crop production data after errors
data.description:
Key points:
  • AI tool to check US crop production report due November 10
  • September data errors affected Nebraska, Kansas yield estimates
  • USDA says AI check will add to, not replace, its data validation

By Tom Polansek

The US Department of Agriculture will use an artificial intelligence tool it built to check data in next week's monthly crop production report, agency officials said, after a series of data missteps eroded farmers' and traders' trust in its forecasts.

After the USDA discovered errors in its corn data from September, officials determined the AI tool would have flagged the problem and decided to use it on the crop production report due on November 10, USDA Under Secretary Scott Hutchins said in an interview.

The tool's debut tests whether the agency can restore confidence in data that often moves markets.

"I'm very bullish on the fact that we'll be able to utilize these tools in the future to help us avoid these kinds of really, truly unfortunate errors," Hutchins said on Thursday.

Last month, the USDA corrected its September corn production and yield data. The correction raised the yield estimate by about 3% in Nebraska, the third-biggest corn-producing state, and lowered it by about 2% in Kansas.

The agency, long viewed as the gold standard of global agricultural market information, previously faced criticism after it made sharp upward revisions to estimates for last year's corn acreage. Over the summer, it reported inaccurate beef export sales data.

The USDA previously said it was launching a pilot project that would rely more heavily on technology to improve crop acreage and yield estimates as fewer farmers respond to its surveys.

COMPUTER FILE ERROR

Lance Honig, chair of the agricultural statistics board for USDA's National Agricultural Statistics Service, told Reuters that a computer file incorrectly combined data on irrigated and non-irrigated corn acres gathered by field surveyors, causing the errors in September's data. Kansas and Nebraska were affected because they have higher percentages of irrigated fields, which often have higher yields, he said.

"This error that occurred in September is literally a very isolated occurrence that, quite frankly, with the proper validation, we should have caught," Honig said. "There was no issue with the data that was gathered at the field level."

The errors angered farmers who are struggling to make money as they pay soaring prices for diesel, fertilizer and other inputs. Last month, the National Corn Growers Association, which represents 35,000 farmers, said the September errors were unacceptable and had further hurt farmers' confidence in the USDA's ability to produce accurate reports.

"You just don't know what the USDA is going to do anymore," said Jim Gerlach, president of brokerage A/C Trading in Indiana, on Friday. "Their reports have become so erratic."

Questions around the credibility of federal data increased after President Donald Trump's administration sharply downsized the government last year. Thousands of employees at the USDA have left, and experts have worried the cuts hobbled the agency's ability to produce accurate and timely data.

Hutchins said the September errors were not related to staffing losses. The new AI tool will add to, not replace, the agency's data validation, he said.

"The tool is basically going to be used as a check to make sure that there are no anomalies that we were not able to see or identify in the normal process," Hutchins said.

This week, market analysts questioned the accuracy of another monthly USDA report on soy processing which showed a sharp divide between how many soybeans were crushed and how much soymeal was produced in Iowa. The USDA said it was reviewing the report as part of a normal process and would make any necessary revisions next month.
